items.title: Barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales: findings from focus groups
items.abstract: Background Building on a previous Wales-wide survey, this study aimed to provide more in-depth exploration of the barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales. Objectives The study aimed to explore these barriers and facilitators among various social groups, to inform policy development in Wales. Methods Four focus groups were conducted with a group of members of the public and a group of healthcare professionals (both groups recruited from a previous survey), as well as a group Sixth Form students and a group of retired adults. Inductive thematic analysis was used to generate themes and to compare the issues raised by the various groups. Contiguity-based analysis was undertaken to underscore how themes related with each other. Results A total of 21 individuals participated in the focus groups (healthcare professionals=6, members of the public=6, sixth-form students=5, retirees=4). Seven thematic networks were identified. Across groups, seven themes were identified in the healthcare professional group, six in the general members of the public group, seven in the sixth form student group, and seven in the retiree group. All groups voiced concerns about data privacy and highlighted the importance of human oversight of AI and human contact during the clinical encounter as they expressed more trust in human practitioners. There were though differences between groups, such as greater trust in black-box systems by healthcare professionals, and between individual participants in regard to trust in private organisations developing AI for healthcare organisations. Conclusions All groups were concerned with information security and expressed a preference for human contact during the clinical encounter and a human-in-the-loop approach. There were differences between the groups, such as in attitudes towards black-box AI technologies and trust in clinicians. No additional barriers or facilitators were identified for proxy consent.

items.title: Basic psychological need satisfaction profiles at work: person-centered links to job crafting and intrinsic motivation
items.abstract: Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study adopted a person-centered approach to investigate whether job crafting behaviors are associated with employees’ membership in basic psychological need satisfaction profiles. Previous research has focused on contextual workplace factors such as job demands-resources and managerial behaviors, with less attention given to employees’ proactive role in influencing their motivational experiences. This study addresses this gap by identifying basic psychological need satisfaction profiles among employees in South African small and medium enterprises. It further examines whether job crafting predicts profile membership and whether these profiles differ in intrinsic motivation. A cross-sectional survey with 197 employees was conducted. They completed the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale–Work Domain, Job Crafting Questionnaire, and Multidimensional Work Motivation Scale. Latent profile analysis supported three quantitatively differentiated profiles reflecting low, moderate, and high need satisfaction. In classification-error-adjusted analyses, job crafting dimensions were associated with profile membership. Higher task and cognitive crafting differentiated the high from the moderate profile, whereas cognitive and relational crafting differentiated the moderate from the low profile. Sensitivity analyses indicated that estimates contrasting the high and low profiles were imprecise and should be interpreted cautiously. Intrinsic motivation differed significantly across the profiles, with employees in the high need satisfaction profile reporting the highest intrinsic motivation. These findings extend person-centered research on SDT by showing that proactive job crafting behaviors are associated with employees’ membership in more adaptive need satisfaction groups.

items.title: Behavioral differentiation during the AIGC image generation waiting period: effects on creativity in conceptual design
items.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) offers new ways to generate inspiration for conceptual design, yet limited attention has been paid to the waiting period between prompt submission and AI image output. This study examined behavioral differentiation during this interval and investigated how the task relevance and cognitive load of waiting-period behaviors affect creativity in conceptual design. Methods Three experiments were conducted with design students. Experiment 1 identified and classified core waiting-period behaviors ( N = 30); Experiment 2 measured the cognitive load of representative behaviors using the NASA-TLX ( N = 24); and Experiment 3 employed a behavior-based 2 × 2 conceptual framework ( N = 60), in which four representative waiting-period behaviors were selected to represent different combinations of task relevance (high/low) and relative workload (higher/lower), and their creative performance was compared. Results The results showed that the AIGC generation waiting period was not a passive interval but involved multiple identifiable behavioral patterns. Creative performance differed across the four representative behavioral conditions. Specifically, the overall creativity score in the GP condition was significantly lower than the scores in the RS, DB, and RB conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed among the latter three conditions. These findings further suggest that the subsequent influence of waiting-period behaviors on creativity may depend not only on the level of cognitive demand but also on whether cognitive resources remain directed toward the ongoing creative task. Discussion This study further interprets AIGC generation waiting-period behaviors from three interrelated functional perspectives: task continuity, cognitive expenditure, and temporary disengagement/incubation. This functional account provides an empirical basis for understanding the cognitive role of the AIGC generation waiting period and for optimizing AI-assisted conceptual design workflows.

items.title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human-machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human-computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human-machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

items.title: Benefits and Drawbacks of Using Artificial Intelligence to Manage Human Resources in the Tourism Industry of Vulnerable Areas: A Case Study of Jammu and Kashmir
items.abstract: This present study examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping Human Resource Management (HRM) within the tourism sector of Jammu and Kashmir, a region that depends heavily on tourism yet faces persistent political and social instability. Drawing insights from 15 semi-structured interviews with HR managers, tourism operators, and employees, the research identifies three major themes: digital literacy, trust deficit, and AI-driven opportunities. While nearly 80% of respondents acknowledged AI&s;s potential to simplify recruitment and enhance training, most also expressed concerns about inconsistent internet access, limited awareness, and job insecurity. The findings suggest that AI, though promising, cannot be viewed as a quick solution. Its successful integration will depend on gradual adoption, transparent practices, and active collaboration among government bodies, HR professionals, and tourism authorities to build AI readiness in such sensitive regions.

items.title: BEYOND AUTOMATION: REFRAMING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN EDUCATION THROUGH COGNITIVE AUTONOMY, ADAPTIVE LEARNING, AND HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is transforming instructional practices, assessment methods, and the relationship between teachers and learners. However, the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by its ability to automate tasks or generate information. This paper examines AI-supported education through three interconnected dimensions: cognitive autonomy, adaptive learning pathways, and human–AI collaboration. Drawing on international research and educational policy frameworks, the study adopts a conceptual and analytical approach to identify opportunities, challenges, and principles for responsible AI integration. Particular attention is given to students' independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, personalized instruction, and teachers' professional judgement. The paper proposes a conceptual model, termed the Attempt–Assist–Evaluate–Transfer model, which encourages learners to attempt tasks independently, receive targeted AI support, evaluate generated information, and transfer their knowledge to unfamiliar situations without assistance. The analysis suggests that effective AI integration requires more than technological access; it requires pedagogical planning, ethical safeguards, and assessment strategies that prioritize genuine learning. The paper concludes that AI should function as a supportive educational resource rather than a substitute for human reasoning or professional teaching.

items.title: Beyond Seamlessness: Mobile AI and Situated Sense-Making
items.abstract: This commentary explores what it means for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to become mobile, as interaction shifts from screen-bound querying to AI participation in the flow of everyday situations. Rather than framing this shift in terms of access or use, it approaches mobile AI through situated sense-making, understood here in terms of the constitution of sense through ongoing activities, embodied cues, social coordination, and mobile communication affordances as AI becomes part of the situation. Starting from a café interaction staged in a promotional video for a future AI device, the commentary confronts corporate claims of seamless interaction with theoretical accounts of situated sense-making. Drawing on mobile communication studies and human–machine communication (HMC), it argues that mobile AI requires a specification of sense-making as HMC's central boundary object: not only as mutual interpretation between users and interfaces but also as a process embedded in ongoing activities and interactions. The commentary develops this argument through three interrelated aspects of situated sense-making—coordination, distribution, and stabilization—showing how mobile AI may reshape participation, redistribute epistemic authority, and steer relevance toward either shared problematization or premature closure. It thereby advances an approach to analyzing and designing embodied AI that foregrounds visible coordination, responsive alignment, and stabilization that remains open to collective deliberation.

items.title: Beyond Technocentrism in AI-Supported Special Education: The PAISEN Model of Teacher-Mediated Inclusive Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new possibilities for inclusive teaching and learning for students with special educational needs (SEN), yet AI-in-SEN research remains largely technocentric, often describing system capabilities without explaining how outputs become pedagogically meaningful. This conceptual paper develops the PAISEN Model (Pedagogical Artificial Intelligence for Special Education Needs) through an integrative synthesis of AI in education, inclusive pedagogy, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and assistive technology. The model proposes a non-deterministic sequence in which AI Teaching Support Systems provide data and adaptive affordances, Teacher Pedagogical Mediation interprets and contextualises them, and an Inclusive Learning Environment translates decisions into accessible participation opportunities. SEN learning outcomes are treated as proposed consequences rather than established effects. Teacher AI competency, institutional support, digital infrastructure, and learner characteristics function as boundary conditions, while an adaptive feedback loop links learner evidence to teacher reflection and instructional adjustment. The novelty of PAISEN lies in making teacher judgement the central explanatory mechanism and separating technology, pedagogical processes, learning conditions and moderators. Theoretically, it bridges AIED and inclusive education; pedagogically, it clarifies differentiated and UDL-aligned AI use without replacing teacher agency; practically, it provides a testable structure for implementation and evaluation. The proposed relationships require empirical validation in authentic SEN settings.

items.abstract: This article explores the pedagogical potential of using artificial intelligence tools to develop individual learning pathways for primary school pupils, taking into account their educational needs, cognitive abilities, and individual learning pace. Particular attention is given to adaptive learning, the personalization of learning tasks, the analysis of learning outcomes, and the timely provision of pedagogical support. The study emphasizes the importance of maintaining the teacher’s leading role in integrating artificial intelligence into primary education, considering children’s developmental and psychological characteristics, ensuring digital safety, and supporting independent thinking. It also examines how the purposeful and pedagogically grounded use of artificial intelligence can improve learning effectiveness, strengthen pupils’ motivation, and support the educational development of every child.

items.title: Bots, Trust, and Generative AI: Framing Communicative Agency in a Small-Language Media Context
items.abstract: This article examines how bots, chatbots, and generative AI are represented as forms of communicative agency in a small-language media environment. It draws on a mixed content analysis of 195 digital news items published by 1TV.ge, Euronews Georgia, Imedi News, and Rustavi 2 between September 15, 2024, and December 31, 2025, a fifteen-and-a-half-month period spanning parts of two calendar years. Rather than evaluating AI systems technically or measuring audience responses, the article analyzes how news coverage assigns roles to automated and AI-based systems through publication patterns, outlet profiles, dominant frames, functional emphases, trust narratives, risk discourse, media literacy elements, and named AI systems. The corpus was most often organized through a technological or business news frame (93 items; 47.7%). Other frames included myth-nightmare (36; 18.5%), media literacy/fact-checking (26; 13.3%), global political competition/information war (24; 12.3%), and myth-idyll (16; 8.2%). The comparison shows that Euronews Georgia emphasized international and security-related coverage, Imedi News foregrounded education and textual interaction, Rustavi 2 emphasized consumer-facing products and visual applications, and 1TV.ge displayed a comparatively balanced explanatory profile. The article argues that bot transformation is better understood as a change in communicative roles than as a simple replacement of older automation by AI chatbots. In this process, agency, usefulness, trust, risk, and responsibility intersect. The Georgian-language case contributes to Human-Machine Communication, AI-mediated communication, and media-framing research by showing how global AI debates are localized outside dominant English-language media environments. Coding was conducted by a single researcher; an intracoder stability check on 20 items (approximately 10% of the corpus) produced no changes to dominant-frame assignments.

items.title: Bridging communication gaps across the biomedical ecosystem
items.abstract: The current landscape of science communication is undergoing rapid transformation, shaped by profound societal shifts including the COVID-19 pandemic, the rise of social media, the decline of traditional news media, and the growing influence of large language models. These changes have fundamentally altered how the biomedical community and the public share, consume, and trust scientific information. This article contextualizes these changes, explains why redesigning the science communication ecosystem is urgent, and offers recommendations to improve accuracy, strengthen trust, and deepen public engagement. Specifically, philanthropy can play a key role by driving momentum and optimizing the flow of scientific information across three stages: (1) scientific discovery to publication, (2) interpretation and distribution, and (3) public engagement.

items.title: Building a Multilingual Legal Risk Database and ClauseRisk Visual Analytics System for Contracts and Online Service Agreements
items.abstract: Documents containing binding legal terms and risk obligations remain largely unread, particularly in multilingual contexts where regulatory systems vary across jurisdictions. This paper presents a multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to identify potentially risky clauses across Arabic, English and French legal, regulatory and contractual documents, instantiated on Algerian legislation as a fully specified reference framework. In addition, we introduce a visual analytics system tailored for legal domain experts, integrating the underlying datasets, model outputs and evaluation results to support interactive analysis and model interpretability. The system’s knowledge base is grounded in a trilingual corpus of 2535 sentences, comprising 315 fully annotated clauses whose cross-lingual legal equivalence was verified by a panel of ten legal experts. Performance evaluation was conducted on EVAL-EEM, an external corpus of 81 annotated passages extracted from 55 real-world sources. Because EVAL-EEM was used during development for decision-configuration tuning, it is characterised as a development corpus rather than a strictly held-out test set; consequently, both in-sample metrics and nested cross-validated estimates are reported. On the binary risk-identification task, the proposed system improves from an initial F1 score of 0.340 to 0.806 in the final in-sample evaluation and 0.792 under nested cross-validation. GPT-4o without retrieval achieves an F1 score of 0.775, showing no statistically significant difference from the complete RAG architecture (p=0.39), whereas supervised baselines, including a fine-tuned XLM-R, exhibit substantially lower performance on external documents. These empirical findings demonstrate the potential of statute-grounded multilingual LLM reasoning augmented by traceable retrieval evidence. However, because configuration selection was conducted on the evaluation corpus itself, these results should be interpreted as preliminary and specific to the evaluated knowledge base, dataset and legal visual analytics system. Further validation on larger, unexposed benchmarks, along with formal user studies, is necessary to establish cross-jurisdictional portability, empirical generalizability and system usability.

items.title: C2 multi-agent factory: large-small model collaboration empowering a new command and control paradigm
items.abstract: Abstract Command and control (C2) is an agile crisis management architecture for highly uncertain emergencies, originating from military operations but now widely deployed in public safety emergency response, traffic and airspace management, industrial energy systems, urban governance, and large-scale event coordination. Traditional C2 systems mainly rely on preset rules, static processes and manual decision-making, which expose obvious limitations in the face of modern environments with high dynamics, complex disturbances and incomplete information. Aiming at the significant problems of traditional command and control systems, such as structural rigidity, information overload, decision lag, and insufficient collaboration, based on the concepts of software factory and single-agent factory, combined with the latest progress of large-small model collaboration in the field of command and control, this paper proposes a new paradigm of large-small model collaboration empowering command and control—the concept of C2 multi-agent factory, which upgrades the single-agent factory that produces “individual intelligence” to a multi-agent factory that produces and runs “swarm intelligence”, and is combined with the command and control system and its application scenarios. The overall system architecture of the C2 multi-agent factory and the large-small model collaboration mechanism based on the C2 multi-agent factory are given. Finally, an application example is given to further illustrate how the C2 multi-agent factory can use the large-small model collaboration technology to empower command and control. The C2 multi-agent factory proposed in this paper will find a new path for the construction of an evolvable intelligent command and control system, promote the substantive leap of artificial intelligence towards the C2 system.

items.title: Calibrating LLM Explanations to Human Decisions with Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Explanations of LLM outputs are considered an important way to make model behavior legible, helping human users make good decisions on downstream tasks. However, default training approaches for improving explanations target model task performance or human preference rather than human decision quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{HD-RL}, a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing LLM explanations for human decision making. Our approach calibrates a human decision simulator on observed human decisions, applying a proxy reward model to optimize the LLM to generate explanations that help people to make good decisions. We apply this framework to AI-generated text detection. In our initial data collection phase, we observed that while LLMs possess strong autonomous detection capabilities, the explanations they generate for users yield near-random human accuracy (51.3\%). By applying the HD-RL framework to the open-source Qwen 3.6 model, we generate optimized explanations that improve human performance, achieving a GLMM-estimated human accuracy of 63.7\% in a randomized between-subjects experiment with repeated measures and outperforming RLVR, RLAIF, and other baselines by over 8\%.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Personalize Learning? An Analysis of AI-Based Adaptive Learning Systems for Senior School Students
items.abstract: Most classrooms still move at one speed. A teacher with thirty or forty students has to choose a pace that suits the middle of the class, which leaves weaker students behind and keeps stronger students waiting. AI-based adaptive learning systems promise to change this by watching how each student answers, estimating what that student already knows, and choosing the next task to match. This paper examines how far that promise holds for senior school students. It explains how adaptive systems work in simple terms, reviews findings from major meta-analyses and field experiments, including a randomised study of the Mindspark program in Delhi, and compares adaptive learning with the traditional one-size-fits-all approach. The evidence suggests that well-designed adaptive systems produce real and sometimes large learning gains, with reported effect sizes between about 0.2 and 0.8 standard deviations, and that students who are furthest behind often gain the most. However, the gains depend heavily on how the system is designed and how it is used. Systems that simply give answers can weaken learning, and results shrink when teachers are not involved. The paper concludes that AI can personalise practice, feedback and pacing to a significant extent, but it cannot replace the motivational, social and judgement-based work of a teacher. A blended model, in which AI handles adaptive practice and teachers use the data to guide instruction, is proposed for Indian senior schools.

items.title: Cardiometabolic Assessment in Patients with Overweight, Obesity, or Type 2 Diabetes Undergoing Artificial Intelligence–Based Retinal Screening: A Real-World Evidence Study
items.abstract: Background: Overweight, obesity, and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) increase the risk of vascular complications, including retinal vascular alterations. Artificial intelligence (AI)—based retinal screening enables early detection of microvascular damage, potentially contributing to appropriate cardiometabolic prevention strategies. We performed a realworld evidence observational study to assess cardiometabolic parameters as well as retinal vascular alterations using novel AI-based retinal imaging. Methods: Between September and December 2025, we recruited 301 consecutive adults with overweight,obesity, or T2DM; cardiometabolic assessment was performed, and all participants also underwent retinal screening with the Aireen AI system, distinguishing those who resulted positive ( n = 42), negative ( n = 204), or undetermined ( n = 55) at the screening. Results: All patients who resulted positive at the screening were confirmed with a diagnosis of retinal alterations by the ophthalmologists. The presence of positive retinal screening (RS+) progressively increased with worsening fasting glycemia, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, carotid intima–media thickness, and endothelial function ( P < 0.001 for all). Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed independent associations of RS+ with HbA1c [odds ratio (OR) 2.29, P < 0.001], carotid stenosis (OR 1.06, P < 0.001), fasting glucose (OR 1.02, P < 0.001), and the triglyceride/high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (OR 2.19, P = 0.010). Conclusions: These findings suggest that AIbased retinal screening with advanced tools can effectively identify early microvascular damage in individuals with overweight, obesity, or T2DM, with RS+ prevalence reflecting glycemic burden and vascular dysfunction. Therefore, integrating AI retinal assessment into cardiometabolic prevention programs may enable timely interventions to prevent progression to vision-threatening complications and support comprehensive cardiovascular risk management.

items.title: Cervical Cancer Burden in Africa: An Integrative Review of Epidemiology, Plant Medicine, and AI-Driven Innovation
items.abstract: Cervical cancer imposes a heavy burden in low- and middle-income countries and persistently high incidence and mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa due to unequal access to prevention and care. Although human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major driving factor, the risk is amplified by HIV co-infection, socioeconomic barriers, limited infrastructure, low health literacy, and behavioral factors, leading to frequent late-stage diagnosis, low screening coverage, and poor survival. Recent expansion of HPV vaccination programs since 2019 has achieved high coverage in some countries, but continent-wide rates remain below targets amid hesitancy, inequities, and systemic weaknesses. Thus, there is a critical need for an integrated synthesis of multidisciplinary evidence that reflects the peculiarities and diversities of African health systems. Moreover, high mortality rates underscore the need for integrated, context-specific evidence to strengthen vaccination, screening, and management strategies in line with WHO global elimination targets. Plant medicine promises to complement mainstream health delivery in low resource settings. Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools show strong potential to improve screening accuracy, reduce subjectivity and resource needs, and enhance early detection in resource-limited settings. This review synthesizes multidisciplinary data on economic impact, epidemiology, risk factors, prevention, diagnostic challenges, plant medicine and AI innovations to guide equitable progress in diverse African contexts.

items.title: Charting the rise of artificial intelligence in medical education: a global bibliometric and network analysis, 2000–2026
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral curiosity to a core feature of modern medical education through adaptive learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, and large language models such as ChatGPT. Publication activity has accelerated rapidly, but the structure of this expanding literature has not been comprehensively mapped. Bibliographic data were obtained from the Web of Science Core Collection using a search strategy that combined medical education terms in the title field with artificial intelligence terms in the topic field. Articles, review articles, and data papers published from 2000 to 2026 were included. A total of 2,298 records were retrieved. Microsoft Excel was used for descriptive analyses, and VOSviewer (version 1.6.20) was used to construct keyword co-occurrence, country collaboration, and institutional collaboration networks. Data for 2026 represent a partial calendar year. Publication output remained limited until the late 2010s and rose sharply after 2021. Of the 2,298 records, 2,066 (89.9%) were published from 2021 to 2026, with the highest complete-year output in 2025 (821 publications). The United States led in publication volume (918 records) and raw citation count (14,582 citations), followed by the People’s Republic of China (367 records; 4,404 citations). The Journal of Surgical Education published the most articles. Harvard Medical School led institutional output, whereas Stanford University and the University of California San Francisco had higher raw citation totals despite fewer publications. Artificial intelligence, medical education, ChatGPT, medical students, and machine learning were the most prominent keywords. Artificial intelligence in medical education is a rapidly expanding but geographically and institutionally concentrated field. Raw citation patterns differed from publication volume, although these unadjusted measures should not be interpreted as direct comparisons of research quality. Thematic patterns emphasize learner-facing applications, assessment, and generative AI, while responsible curricular integration and empirical evaluation remain important priorities. These findings are especially relevant to emergency medicine education, where simulation, time-sensitive decision-making, and competency assessment are central.

items.title: ChatGPT adoption and responsible use in Vietnamese transnational education students’ academic writing
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how cognitive and affective factors drive Vietnamese transnational education (TNE) students' intention to use ChatGPT for English academic writing, and investigates how information verification and responsible use enhance English writing proficiency (EWP). Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 501 TNE students across three major Vietnamese cities were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The conceptual model integrates the technology acceptance model, the pupils’ attitudes toward technology short questionnaire (PATT-SQ) model and Mitcham’s philosophical framework. Insights from an expert survey of six lecturers supported the interpretation and practical implications. Findings Cognitive factors (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and perceived risk) significantly influence ChatGPT usage intention, whereas affective factors do not. Perceived risk negatively impacts intention, reflecting student awareness of potential drawbacks. The results further reveal a strong behavioural pathway in which frequent use intention promotes information verification, which fosters responsible use and ultimately improves EWP. This demonstrates that learning outcomes depend on critical, ethical engagement rather than usage frequency alone. Research limitations/implications Higher education institutions (HEI) should embed AI literacy, verification practices and ethical guidelines into curricula to optimise ChatGPT utility and mitigate dependency. Limitations include a cross-sectional design, lack of contextual factors and a localised sample, which future longitudinal and comparative studies should address. Originality/value This study offers one of the first empirical examinations linking ChatGPT adoption, verification behaviours, responsible use and measurable EWP gains among Vietnamese TNE students. By integrating cognitive, affective, behavioural and ethical dimensions, it extends traditional technology adoption models to the context of generative AI-assisted academic writing.

items.title: Cloud-Based Infrastructure for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Workloads: A Scalable Framework for Saudi Enterprises
items.abstract: In Saudi companies artificial intelligence and machine learning are moving from being mere experiments to becoming operational capabilities, which is leading to an infrastructure issue that goes well beyond the need for computing power. The processes involved in training, fine-tuning, inference, feature preparation, model monitoring, governance and retraining all have diverse requirements for accelerators, storage, networking, data locality, elasticity and reliability. This review draws on research carried out between 2020 and 2025 in order to look at how cloud architecture can support these types of workloads on an enterprise level while taking into account the Saudi situation regarding rapid digital transformation, the adoption of cloud services, data governance and the modernisation of various sectors. The review applies a structured evidence-synthesis approach focused on infrastructure architecture, workload orchestration, MLOps, cloud-edge distribution, security, reliability, cost control and organisational readiness. The evidence shows that scalable AI infrastructure should be viewed as a coordinated platform rather than as a set of separate services; effective designs incorporate elastic pools of CPU and GPU resources, container orchestration, tiered data services, automated model pipelines, observability, policy controls, workload-aware scheduling and selective edge execution. The Saudi Enterprise AI Cloud Framework proposed in this review combines these capabilities into six layers and includes a closed operational loop that links demand prediction, placement, execution, telemetry, policy evaluation and lifecycle learning. The review maintains that scalability must be assessed together with availability, cost predictability, data sovereignty, operational resilience and discipline in managing the model lifecycle. It ends with an implementation roadmap and a research agenda for businesses that wish to industrialise AI as part of their digital transformation aligned with Vision 2030.

items.title: Comparative Deep Learning and RISE-Based Explainable AI Framework for Orange Fruit Disease Detection
items.abstract: Orange diseases significantly threaten fruit quality and agricultural productivity, resulting in substantial economic losses. Traditional diagnostic methods are limited by their labor-intensive nature, high costs, and reliance on subjective expert evaluation, increasing the demand for automated solutions. This study systematically compared three state-of the-art deep learning architectures-EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Tiny, and Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16)-on the Orange Fruit dataset, which comprises healthy, citrus canker, and melanose samples. To enhance generalization and mitigate overfitting, transfer learning with ImageNet pretraining was combined with advanced data augmentation strategies like Mixup and Cutout. Experimental results demonstrated that the ConvNeXt-Tiny architecture, supported by these techniques, achieved superior performance, reaching 98.76% Accuracy, 99% F1-Score, and 99.95% ROC-AUC. Beyond numerical metrics, model transparency was investigated using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The study evaluated the widely used Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) method alongside Randomized Input Sampling for Explanation (RISE), which, to the best of our knowledge, represents one of the first applications of RISE in plant disease image analysis. RISE provided more comprehensive visualizations of the fruit surface regions influencing decisions, thereby strengthening interpretability. These findings confirm the high potential of modern deep learning for early disease diagnosis and highlight that XAI integration significantly enhances the reliability of agricultural decision support systems. Five fold cross-validation experiments and paired t-test analysis further confirmed the robustness and statistical significance of these findings.

items.title: Comparative evaluation of artificial intelligence-based and pathologist scoring of murine bile duct hyperplasia
items.abstract: Bile duct hyperplasia in rodents, caused by chemical cytotoxicity, bile flow interference, or aging, is traditionally assessed through time-consuming microscopic examination by pathologists. We developed a deep learning-based, artificial intelligence (AI) model for quick and accurate assessment of bile duct hyperplasia in mice. The study utilized 127 hematoxylin and eosin-stained, mouse liver whole-slide images (WSIs) digitized using Aperio scanners. A segmentation algorithm with a U-Net architecture and an EfficientNet backbone was trained on 1165 areas from 35 WSIs to identify and quantify bile ducts, measure their area percentage using a supervised method, and categorize them into grades 0 to 4 using an unsupervised method. The model was validated on 24 WSIs and tested on 68 WSIs, all independently scored by 3 veterinary pathologists using consensus criteria. The segmentation model achieved Dice scores of 91.75% in training and 85.88% in validation. Testing revealed high sensitivity (95%), specificity (97%), and Dice score (95.45%), indicating robust model accuracy. Model-predicted grades showed strong correlation ( r 2 s = 0.86) with pathologists’ consensus scores. This AI-driven approach has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of bile duct hyperplasia assessments in rodent studies, paving the way for more standardized, objective, and high-throughput histological evaluations in preclinical research.

items.title: Comparison of AI-Based and Traditional Pencil Drawing Techniques in Terms of Creativity and Artistic Expression
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of Midjourney and DALLE-3, artificial intelligence-based visual production programs, on the creative thinking and artistic expression levels of art teacher candidates. The research was conducted with experimental and control groups consisting of ten students enrolled in the Art Education program at Sivas Cumhuriyet University. The experimental group produced traditional charcoal drawings, while the control group produced AI-assisted charcoal drawings. Data were collected through qualitative comparative analysis and quantitative surveys, analyzed using SPSS, and the similarities and differences between the two approaches were evaluated. The findings obtained within the scope of the research show that manual charcoal applications have a stronger impact on students' artistic expression depth, aesthetic decision-making processes, and experience-based learning gains than artificial intelligence programs. It has been determined that traditional techniques provide a holistic contribution, especially in terms of tactile feedback, error, tolerance process, and individual application process. In contrast, AI-supported production programs were found to offer distinct advantages in terms of technical accuracy, time management, alternative composition generation, and visual variation development. In this context, AI applications were observed to accelerate the creative process and provide technical support. The results, based on the findings, indicate that AI-based visual production programs are complementary tools rather than replacements for traditional art education.

items.title: Conceptualisations of the roles and competencies of ambulance drivers in emergency medical services: A scoping review
items.abstract: Background The ambulance-driving function is essential to safe and timely emergency medical services (EMS). However, competencies associated with ambulance driving remain fragmented and vary across EMS workforce models, in which driving may be performed by dedicated ambulance drivers or incorporated into broader roles such as emergency medical technicians and paramedics. Aim This scoping review aimed to map and synthesise how the roles and competencies associated with ambulance driving are conceptualised across EMS systems. Method The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, GARUDA and Google Scholar were searched. Studies involving ambulance drivers or other prehospital personnel were included when ambulance driving or emergency vehicle operation was explicitly addressed. Data were synthesised using descriptive mapping, thematic synthesis, conceptual framework mapping and gap analysis. Results Nineteen studies published between 2007 and 2026 were included from Europe, Asia, the Middle East and South America. Seven competency domains were identified: technical driving; safety and risk management; cognitive and decision-making; communication and teamwork; stress and emotional management; professional and personal attributes and work ability and fitness. Additional competencies included first aid, basic life support, emergency response and patient-related responsibilities, although these varied across workforce models. Overall, ambulance-driving competency was conceptualised as a multidimensional and context-dependent construct extending beyond vehicle-handling skills to include non-technical skills, human factors and adaptive performance. No comprehensive and standardised competency framework specific to the ambulance-driving function was identified. Conclusions Ambulance driving involves multiple competency domains, while the capability to adapt and apply these competencies is influenced by professional role and EMS context. The seven domains identified provide an evidence-derived conceptual structure rather than a definitive competency framework. Future research should explore how capability, adaptive expertise, human factors and system context can inform competency framework development, education, assessment, workforce development and safety.

items.title: ConSolv: Solvent-Conditional Machine Learning Implicit Solvent Potential
items.abstract: Abstract Implicit solvent machine learning potentials (MLPs) offer a powerful route to bridging the gap between accuracy and efficiency in molecular simulations. However, existing models have largely focused on aqueous environments, overlooking the diverse and important roles of nonaqueous solvents in areas such as organic synthesis and battery technology. Here, we present ConSolv, a solvent-conditional MLP architecture that explicitly incorporates solvent effects on solute interactions through an attention-based solvent embedding block. By combining experimental solvation free energy data with ab initio data, we train a single implicit solvent MLP that is transferable across 66 common organic solvents. ConSolv outperforms classical explicit solvent methods and selected ab initio implicit solvent approaches across multiple solvation free energy benchmarks, and demonstrates generalization to unseen solvents. Beyond solvation free energies, the model shows close agreement with experimental nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data for γ-fluorohydrin molecules in chloroform. ConSolv’s architecture is readily extensible to broader chemical spaces and alternative training strategies, while its attention-based design supports explainable artificial intelligence (AI) analysis that can help elucidate complex, solvent-dependent molecular interactions.

items.title: Construction of Metaverse City, Features, Future and Challenges
items.abstract: The Metaverse 3D Virtual City constitutes the leading-edge manifestation of the broader metaverse, advanced purposely to mirror and enrich the lived experience of physical cities through a wholly immersive digital fabric. This domain develops rapidly, integrating advanced virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and artificial intelligence (AI) to produce interactive strata in which individuals participate in communal, commercial, and recreational domains. Its rapid rise is more than a mere technological spectacle; it materializes as a tectonic shift in the modality of urban experience, widening thresholds for public agency, transactional exchange, and inter-cultural conversation. Contemporary manifestations of the Metaverse, when subjected to retrospective examination, reveal them to be the latest articulation of a virtual urban lineage whose detail and capacity have expanded in concert with the incremental sophistication of technological affordances. Pioneer environments, which restricted participants to textual interaction and minimalist pixel representations, have now evolved into complex three-dimensional ecosystems that transpose the stylistic and operational codes of architecture and urban planning originally conceived for the corporeal city.

items.title: CORRELATION BETWEEN SAFETY AWARENESS AND OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH RISK FACTORS AMONG WASTE WORKERS IN SELECTED GOVERNMENT HOSPITALS IN NIGER-DELTA
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the correlation between safety awareness and occupational health risk among waste workers in selected government hospitals in Niger-Delta region. Safety awareness was operationalized using modified safety awareness scores while knowledge of occupational health risk exposure was captured using physical factors, biomechanical factors, biological Factors and psychosocial factors. Cross-sectional and inferential designs were adopted. The population comprised hospital waste workers in three selected government hospitals in Niger-Delta States namely Imo, Rivers and Akwa-Ibom State. Data collection was done using questionnaire designed based on a 5-point Likert. Data analysis was done using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation. The results of the descriptive statistics using weighted average (WA) revealed that knowledge of waste workers on occupational health risk factor is good (WA = 4.09 > 3.00) and the waste workers have substantial level of safety awareness (WA = 3.76>3.00) The Pearson correlation revealed that positive and significant relationship exists between safety awareness, physical factors and psychosocial factors. The results also showed that there is positive but insignificant relationship between safety awareness and biomechanical factor (BMF) however, safety awareness has negative and significant relationship with biological factors (BF). It was therefore concluded that safety awareness has a positive relationship with occupational health risk factors among waste workers in government-owned hospitals in the Niger-Delta. items.abstract: Every week, a university announces a new course on Large Language Models. Every week, a research lab publishes a new paper on LLMs. Every week, a student pays tuition, or signs up for free, to learn how LLMs work. The question this paper asks is simple:Should any of this be happening?Not "is it useful." Not "does it work." Those are different questions, with different answers.The question here is narrower, and sharper:Is there a scientific foundation under the thing being taught and studied?If there is, then yes — teach it, research it, build a discipline. If there isn't, then somethingelse is happening, and we should name it. This paper argues: the foundation is not scientific. And it shows what that means, plainly, with sources.

items.title: Current status of medical students’ use of large language models for graduation thesis writing: a comparative cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Objective Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a conceptual framework, this study explored medical students’ use of large language models (LLMs) in graduation thesis writing, focusing on application patterns, perceptions, and potential risks. Methods A comparative cross-sectional questionnaire survey using convenience sampling was conducted among medical graduates from medical schools in China in 2024 and 2025. The self-designed 25-item questionnaire included five-point Likert items on perceived advantages and disadvantages of LLMs. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's α , exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was performed, and univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with LLMs use. Results A total of 341 valid questionnaires were collected. Overall, 54.25% (185/341) of respondents reported using LLMs in graduation thesis writing, with use reported by 27.37% (52/190) in 2024 and 88.08% (133/151) in 2025. ChatGPT was the most frequently used platform in 2024 (82.69%, 43/52), whereas Deepseek was the most frequently used platform in 2025 (88.72%, 118/133). LLMs were used primarily during the literature review stage (74.05%, 137/185), mainly to provide writing suggestions (82.16%, 152/185). Cronbach's α was 0.720 for perceived advantages and 0.650 for perceived disadvantages, and exploratory factor analysis identified a two-factor clustering pattern consistent with the predefined grouping of perceived advantages and disadvantages. Among LLMs users, 68.65% (127/185) believed that LLMs use would not compromise academic integrity, whereas 47.57% (88/185) remained concerned about potential academic misconduct. The main perceived disadvantages included the risk of academic misconduct, limited content accuracy, and data privacy and security concerns. The findings were discussed with reference to TAM-related concepts as an interpretive framework. Conclusion LLMs use was substantially higher in the 2025 survey than in the 2024 survey. Although LLMs improve writing efficiency and provide valuable writing support, concerns regarding academic integrity, content accuracy, and data privacy remain important considerations. The TAM provides a useful framework for interpreting students’ adoption patterns and may inform the development of AI education and governance strategies in medical education.

items.title: Cybersecurity Responsibilities in Enterprise Generative AI Adoption: A Qualitative Documentary Analysis of Delegated Authority and Organizational Oversight
items.abstract: Enterprise generative artificial intelligence assistants can retrieve organizational information, recommend decisions, and initiate actions through connected tools. These capabilities make cybersecurity a question of how authority and responsibility are distributed across systems and organizations. This study examines how public guidance translates security responsibilities into controls over enterprise AI assistants. A purposive corpus of 12 documentary units from public bodies, a security community, and technology providers was retrieved on 28 September 2026. Focused qualitative document analysis combined six initial coding categories with cross-document comparison, producing a register of 27 evidence records. Four interpretive themes were developed: responsibility is allocated at different organizational and technical levels; permission inheritance requires contextual judgment about appropriate access; human oversight depends on enforceable intervention points; and incident accountability requires continuity across organizational and temporal boundaries. Counterevidence matters: the corpus contains explicit oversight, authorization, and incident-management provisions, so it does not support a general claim that AI security guidance lacks responsibility requirements. The analysis instead identifies an implementation translation problem between broad obligations, application-level controls, and locally assigned decision rights. A proposed governance framework links retrieval, recommendation, and action capabilities to permission boundaries, intervention conditions, accountable owners, and retained decision evidence. The framework is an analytical synthesis, not an empirically validated maturity model. The study contributes a focused account of responsibility at transitions between AI capabilities and offers an auditable structure for enterprise deployment decisions. Its conclusions concern the selected documents and do not establish organizational compliance, control effectiveness, or industry-wide prevalence.

items.title: Cybersecurity, Network Security, and Privacy: A Theoretical Evaluation
items.abstract: Digital transformation has dissolved the boundaries on which conventional network security was built. Cloud platforms, remote work, mobile endpoints, and the Internet of Things have turned organizational networks into distributed, hyper-connected ecosystems in which the perimeter-based “castle-and-moat” model can no longer separate trusted from untrusted entities. Once inside such a perimeter, adversaries exploit implicit trust to move laterally, and they increasingly use algorithmic tools to automate reconnaissance and attack. At the same time, defensive architectures that depend on pervasive monitoring collide with legal and ethical obligations to protect communication privacy. Within the context of algorithmic transformation, this chapter offers a theoretical evaluation of cybersecurity, network security, and privacy. Drawing on recent literature, standards, and national and international governance frameworks, it examines three interrelated themes: the shift from perimeter defense to Zero Trust Architecture and its operationalization through microsegmentation in virtualized, containerized, and multi-cloud environments; the role of network observability, deep packet inspection, and Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems in correlating distributed telemetry; and the dilemma between comprehensive end-to-end monitoring and the preservation of privacy. The analysis shows that continuous verification, least privilege, and an assume-breach posture cannot be enforced through static rules alone; their practical viability depends on artificial intelligence and machine learning that establish behavioral baselines, adjust trust dynamically, synthesize segmentation policies, and orchestrate automated responses through SIEM, Extended Detection and Response (XDR), and Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms. The chapter treats privacy as an architectural design constraint rather than a regulatory burden and discusses how Privacy by Design, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, and federated learning can reconcile intelligent defense with data protection. Its central contribution is a conceptual reconciliation of the security-privacy trade-off: by shifting from payload inspection to encrypted traffic analysis and endpoint-centric telemetry, organizations can retain the visibility that Zero Trust requires without breaking end-to-end encryption. For security governance, this implies that cybersecurity must become a continuous, identity-driven organizational capability. The chapter also identifies the need for empirical validation against adversarial evasion and for explainable, auditable autonomous defense, and it outlines future research on autonomous policy synthesis, post-quantum Zero Trust, edge-native federated telemetry, and formal verification of defensive AI models.

items.title: D2.1. National AI Stakeholder and Market Landscape Report
items.abstract: Executive Summary Serbia’s artificial intelligence (AI) landscape is evolving rapidly. It is being shaped by parallel advances in digitalisation, innovation, industrial adoption and emerging regulatory frameworks. In recent years, the country has invested in modernising public services, strengthening its research and innovation capacity, and supporting the growth of high-tech companies and start-ups. These developments have created a foundation for the more systematic and large-scale deployment of AI across key sectors, including Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language domains, where growing technological capabilities and a progressively more mature ecosystem can be developed. The primary objective of this report is to establish an empirical and analytical foundation for positioning Serbian Artificial Intelligence Factory Antenna (SAIFA) as the central national mechanism for integrating the Serbian AI ecosystem into the wider European high-performance computing (Europa) value chain. In strict alignment with the project proposal's description, the deliverable provides a detailed mapping of Serbian AI ecosystem actors, business domains, regulatory drivers, and barriers to adoption, alongside a dedicated focus on four priority verticals: Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language. The report is structured to provide a comprehensive assessment of Serbia’s emerging AI ecosystem, combining desk-based analysis with planned field research. It first presents the methodology applied throughout the assessment, including the main analytical approaches, data sources and criteria used for mapping and evaluating the national AI landscape. The subsequent sections present the findings of the desktop research, including an assessment of the Serbian AI landscape and an analysis of stakeholders relevant to the SAIFA project. The AI landscape assessment covers four key dimensions of the national AI ecosystem: research & education, industry & commercial AI activities, regulatory framework, and computational infrastructure. The stakeholder analysis, in turn, identifies the organization’s and stakeholder groups relevant to SAIFA, examining their roles, capabilities, needs and potential contribution to the project and its activities. Starting in September 2026, the assessment will be complemented by field research involving interviews, surveys and focus groups with different stakeholder groups. This research will provide a more in-depth understanding of the barriers, needs, opportunities and potential for AI development and adoption in Serbia, complementing the evidence gathered through the desktop analysis. The findings from the field research will subsequently be consolidated and disseminated through dedicated thematic SAIFA White Papers, providing evidence-based insights into AI readiness, adoption barriers, user needs and development opportunities in selected areas. The results will also be formally incorporated into Deliverable D2.3, ensuring that the evidence collected through field research feeds directly into the subsequent stages of the SAIFA project. The entire research architecture is designed to remain coherent with international benchmarks and the engagement models of sister European AI Factories, specifically Pharos and IT4LIA, while ensuring strict compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and data management protocols. Alongside this report, a structured Serbian AI Ecosystem Database was developed, providing a tabular overview of AI-related scientific and research projects, publications by authors affiliated with Serbian institutions, patent applications, study programmes, AI companies, ecosystem enablers, support programmes, regulatory frameworks and regulatory-development initiatives, public institutions, and national AI and computing infrastructure. The database is designed to be made publicly accessible through the SAIFA website and to serve as a living resource that can be regularly updated as the Serbian AI ecosystem evolves. The assessment of macroeconomic and general digital preconditions positions Serbia as a fast-advancing adopter and the leading Western Balkan (WB) economy in AI readiness. This trajectory is underpinned by a highly competitive Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector, which achieved a record export surplus and an all-time high total export value of €4.55 billion in 2025 (OITEG, 2026). However, a granular evaluation across the four conceptual pillars of the AI ecosystem reveals deep structural asymmetries: · Research, Innovation and Education: Serbia has introduced foundational AI components across primary and secondary curricula and accredited nine specialized AI-focused degree programs since 2021. Scientific publication output has experienced a sharp expansion, exceeding 450 AI-related papers in 2025. Conversely, the commercialization of this knowledge remains a critical bottleneck; only 66 AI-related patent applications were filed between 2017 and mid-2026, highlighting a weak technology-transfer pipeline from academia to market. · Industry and Firm-Level Intensity: The domestic AI business landscape comprises approximately 300 developers and integrators. Startups and Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs) form the dominant core, accounting for 89% of these firms, showcasing high agility and an entrepreneurial drive that culminated in the emergence of Serbia’s first tech unicorn (Ominimo) in 2026. However, the corporate and venture capital layers are thin. Venture capital (VC) expenditure stands at a critical low of 8.0% of the EU average, leaving the startup base heavily reliant on public grants and personal funds, which severely restricts their ability to scale commercially. · Regulation and Governance: Serbia has actively established strategic policy intent, moving from its initial Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia (SDAIRS) (2020–2025) and Ethical Guidelines to a comprehensive new SDAIRS for the Period 2025–2030. In the absence of specialized legislation, AI is currently governed by a distributed matrix of horizontal laws (data protection, cybersecurity, non-discrimination). The upcoming draft Law on Artificial Intelligence, largely aligned with the EU AI Act, signals Serbia’s move towards a more comprehensive AI regulatory framework. · Computational Infrastructure: Serbia’s computational infrastructure is developing rapidly, with significant investments in national AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) capacity. Hosted at the Government Data Center in Kragujevac (GDCK), the National AI Platform has reached a combined operational capacity of 37 PFLOPS using NVIDIA A100 and H200 GPU architectures. The planned delivery of a third supercomputer based on NVIDIA Grace Hopper technology in early 2027 will further strengthen Serbia’s national AI and computing capacity. This report also provides a systematic Stakeholder Analysis, categorising ecosystem actors according to their functional roles within the AI ecosystem. The analysis distinguishes four main groups: Data Providers and Domain Experts (public institutions, utilities and industrial organisations holding valuable datasets and domain knowledge), AI Researchers and Model Developers (universities and research institutes providing methodological and machine-learning expertise), AI Application Developers (startups and software companies turning AI capabilities into applications), and End-Users and Beneficiaries (e.g. patients, farmers, businesses and public administrations whose needs define the objectives of AI solutions). The analysis is complemented by cross-cutting ecosystem enablers and intermediaries, including science and technology parks, industry associations, chambers, incubators and accelerators, as well as investors, funding organisations and public authorities. Their role is particularly important for matchmaking, dissemination, funding, regulation and creating the conditions for collaboration. Sector-specific analyses were conducted for healthcare, energy, environment & sustainability, and language & culture, identifying relevant stakeholder groups, concrete organisations, and the resources they can contribute or require. Illustrative use cases, presented in this section, demonstrate how organisations with complementary data, domain expertise, AI capabilities and market access can be connected through SAIFA. The analysis therefore proposes stakeholder engagement activities focused on turning connections into concrete projects, including thematic workshops and roundtables, AI-focused forums and hackathons, direct outreach and bilateral meetings, SAIFA information sessions, and participation in sector-specific and scientific events. Together, these activities position SAIFA not only as an AI and HPC service provider, but as a facilitator of collaboration, resource exchange and joint solution development across Serbia’s AI ecosystem. Serbia’s strongest AI potential lies in HealthTech and BioTech, as well as in environment and sustainability, where established research capacities, relevant data, industry demand and an emerging base of technology providers provide a solid foundation for further development. At the same time, culture & language, as well as cybersecurity, represent emerging high-potential areas, characterised by a growing number of AI-related projects, research activities and companies, although their ecosystem bases are currently less developed. These areas therefore offer significant opportunities for targeted ecosystem-building and are particularly relevant to SAIFA’s project priorities. The ecosystem is geographically concentrated around Belgrade, Novi Sad, Niš and Kragujevac, with major Research and Development (R&D) and computing capacities centred on leading universities, research institutes and national infrastructure. items.title: D3.1. Design of the AI Gateway
items.abstract: Executive Summary Context. The Serbian AI Factory Antenna (SAIFA) is a HORIZON-JU-EuroHPC project (Grant Agreement No. 101263280) that establishes a national entry point to artificial intelligence and high-performance computing for research and clinical institutions, industry, the public sector and individual users. The AI Gateway is developed in Work Package 3, Task 3.4, as the unified access point for AI resources, tools and services. Deliverable D3.1, due in M03, provides the comprehensive initial plan for its development. Scope. The design covers access to computing environments, datasets, pre-trained models, applications, reusable tools, modular workflows, training materials and support services. It also addresses authentication, resource scheduling, monitoring, secure sharing and interoperability with national infrastructure, Pharos, IT4LIA, the AI-on-Demand Platform and other AI Factory services. The design sets out a target direction and an evaluation process. It does not predetermine the final implementation scope, architecture or division of responsibilities, nor does it commit the project consortium to delivering every described capability or workflow in the beta or subsequent releases. Design approach. The Gateway is conceived as a modular integration and control layer rather than a monolithic platform. Mature components are reused for identity management, cataloguing, notebooks, model management, execution, storage, monitoring and learning. SAIFA-specific development is concentrated on the unified portal, common metadata and authorisation rules, quota and accounting logic, the HPC bridge, audit, and federation adapters. Users and use cases. The functional scope is illustrated through 21 Domain Use Stories covering language and culture, biomedicine and health, energy and manufacturing, environment, and cross-domain adoption. A representative set of system use cases specifies the principal interactions for authentication, discovery, data and model management, compute jobs, inference, experiments, training, federation and support. These descriptions remain subject to validation and prioritisation with domain owners, infrastructure operators and user-support teams. Technology and risk. Candidate technologies are evaluated through short proofs of concept, mandatory elimination criteria and comparative assessment of usability, integration effort, operational complexity, performance, maturity, compliance and sustainability. The accompanying risk register combines proposal-level risks with Gateway-specific security, integration, data-integrity and operational risks, and links them to preventive controls and acceptance evidence. Roadmap. The contractual path is D3.1 in M03, access to national infrastructure in M03, access and use policies and the online beta version in M12, and D3.4 - AI gateway functionalities and features - in M18. Task 3.4 continues through M36, covering further integration, hardening, interoperability, validation and operational improvement. Development and preliminary testing are carried out on the PARADOX and ITE infrastructures, followed by validation and benchmarking using the Greek and Italian AI Factory infrastructures. Outcome. Together, these documents form a coherent design baseline that links the project structure, domain needs, system behaviour, candidate technologies, delivery plan and risk controls. The baseline supports implementation while preserving the flexibility needed to incorporate validated user requirements and evidence from the planned proofs of concept.

items.title: Data Management and Integration in Precision Agriculture
items.abstract: Precision agriculture (PA) leverages modern technologies to enhance productivity, optimize resource use, and reduce environmental impact. Efficient data management and integration play a critical role in PA, as large volumes of data are generated through Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven analytics. This chapter explores various methodologies used to manage, integrate, and utilize agricultural data effectively, emphasizing cloud computing, blockchain, and decision support systems (DSS). We discuss the challenges and future directions of data-driven agriculture to promote sustainability and efficiency. In recent years, a wide range of technologies has been integrated into PA to enhance crop monitoring and management. These advancements aim to improve sustainability while maximizing yield and quality. However, many available technologies and standards have yet to be fully incorporated into these practices. As a result, the potential synergy between breeding and agronomic expertise, electronics, and computing has not been entirely realized. Emerging and established technologies, such as the Internet of Everything (IoE), IoT, cloud and fog computing, alongwith cost-effective, low-power computing devices, and wireless communication methods, have made it possible to rapidly develop and implement innovative monitoring solutions. items.title: Data-driven risk assessment of occupational accidents in Indonesian open-pit coal mining using regression and neural network modeling
items.abstract: Background Occupational accidents in open-pit mining remain a significant workplace safety and public health concern due to hazardous environmental conditions, high-risk tasks, and complex human–organizational interactions. Data-driven risk modeling may enhance accident prevention and occupational health management. Objective To identify key determinants of occupational accidents in an open-pit coal mining operation and develop a predictive risk assessment model to support injury prevention and safety decision-making. Methods A retrospective quantitative study was conducted using accident records (2017–2024) from a large open-pit mining company. Variables included accident timing, location, department, job position, age, work experience, unsafe acts, unsafe conditions, personal factors, and job-related factors. Multivariate regression and artificial neural network (ANN) modeling were applied to examine associations and predict the number of affected workers. Model performance was evaluated using correlation coefficients, mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute deviation (MAD), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and bias. Results Unsafe acts, hazardous environments, low worker motivation, and inadequate supervision were dominant risk contributors. Regression analysis showed significant associations between accident variables and injury occurrence ( p < 0.05). The ANN model demonstrated strong predictive performance (overall R = 0.973; testing R = 0.992) with low error (MSE = 0.015; MAPE = 13.2%), while the linear regression model explained comparatively little variance ( R 2 = 0.094), indicating that occupational risk in this setting is driven predominantly by nonlinear interactions among behavioral, environmental, and organizational factors. Accidents were more frequent among operators, workers aged 26–30 years, and employees with >5 years of experience. Conclusions Integrating statistical and machine learning approaches provides a structured framework for identifying occupational risk patterns. Predictive modeling can support targeted supervision, behavioral safety interventions, and hazard control strategies in high-risk industrial settings.

items.title: Deep Acoustic Classification of Aircraft and Engine Types Using CNN–LSTM Models: Spectral–temporal Analysis, Cross-validation, and Performance Benchmarking
items.abstract: Detecting aircraft engine types has a wide range of applications in both defense and civilian sectors. In military settings, identifying the engine type of an aircraft helps distinguish between passenger platforms and potential threats, enabling appropriate situational response. Recognizing the aircraft category from its acoustic signature is also crucial for real-time situational awareness and sound-based monitoring. On the civilian side, airports and urban authorities use acoustic identification to monitor overhead aircraft, manage air traffic, and assess environmental noise impacts. In this study, we propose a deep learning–based model to classify aircraft into four categories: passenger airplane, drone, fighter jet, and helicopter. Log-frequency cepstral coefficients (LFCCs) are extracted as input features and fed into a custom hybrid architecture combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers. To evaluate performance, we applied 5-fold cross-validation and compared the proposed model with several baselines, including standard CNN, CNN-LSTM, CNN-GRU, CNN-RNN, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers. Experimental results show that our model outperforms all baselines in classification accuracy. The proposed model achieved an overall accuracy of 82.65% for the four-class task. After applying temporal consistency smoothing as a post-processing step, overall accuracy improved to 83.40%, with passenger airplane accuracy increasing from 70.7% to 73.44% and fighter accuracy from 81.5% to 84.62%. The binary engine-type classification task achieved 84.15% accuracy, which remained unchanged after smoothing. An ablation study confirmed the synergistic effect of combining CNN and LSTM components, as the CNN-only and LSTM-only models achieved only 61.4% and 53.9% accuracy, respectively.

items.title: Deep Learning and Artificial Intelligence: Conceptual Foundations of Pattern Recognition and Security Applications
items.abstract: The rapid growth of digital data and the increasing complexity of security threats have expanded the use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in modern security systems. This chapter presents the conceptual foundations of deep learning and pattern recognition and examines their roles in security-oriented applications. It first clarifies the relationships among artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and pattern recognition, emphasizing the transition from manually engineered features to representation learning through multilayer neural networks. Fundamental mechanisms of deep learning, including artificial neurons, activation functions, forward propagation, backpropagation, loss functions, and hierarchical representation learning, are subsequently discussed. The chapter also reviews major deep learning architectures, including Multilayer Perceptrons, Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, Autoencoders, and Transformers, with particular attention to their suitability for different data types and security problems. Their applications are examined in the context of intrusion detection, anomaly detection, malware detection, phishing detection, security log analysis, and physical and biometric security. Recent developments involving large language models, federated learning, Edge AI, and continual learning are also considered as emerging directions for security analysis. Beyond predictive performance, the chapter emphasizes that reliable artificial intelligence-based security systems must address several limitations and risks. These include data quality and representativeness, class imbalance, overfitting, data and concept drift, adversarial attacks, data poisoning, model extraction, and membership inference attacks. The discussion further highlights the importance of explainability, privacy, algorithmic fairness, robustness, and human oversight, particularly in high-risk security environments where incorrect decisions may have significant consequences. Overall, the chapter argues that artificial intelligence and security have a bidirectional relationship: artificial intelligence can strengthen threat detection and decision support, while AI systems themselves may become targets of malicious manipulation. Future security systems are therefore expected to rely increasingly on trustworthy, explainable, privacy-aware, adaptive, and human-supervised approaches that combine advanced pattern recognition capabilities with operational and ethical safeguards.
