items.title: Exploring nursing students’ experiences of using generative AI for emotional intelligence learning: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Background Emotional intelligence is a core competency for nursing students; however, traditional nursing education faces challenges in fostering emotional intelligence, including curricular imbalances, limited teaching methods, and delayed assessment and feedback. The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for addressing the above issues; however, existing research has not yet thoroughly explored how nursing students learn emotional intelligence through GenAI or their experiences in this process. Objective Based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Teaching Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, and using Goleman’s five-dimensional model of emotional intelligence as a reference, this study explores the experiences of undergraduate nursing students in using generative artificial intelligence for emotional intelligence learning, as well as the factors that facilitate this process. Method This study employed a qualitative descriptive research design and Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA). Using purposive sampling, 19 undergraduate nursing students (from freshman to senior year) were selected for one-on-one semi-structured in-depth interviews. All participants had experience using GenAI tools (such as DeepSeek and Doubao) for communication practice, case discussions, or sentiment analysis. The interview data were analyzed using the RTA six-stage process, with NVivo 12.0 software used to assist with data management. Results We identified and synthesized 238 initial codes into three core themes. Theme 1, “From Efficiency-Driven to Precise Empathy,” presents the differing descriptions of empathy-related experiences among students in different grade levels: lower-grade students more frequently reported efficiency-driven usage experiences; some middle-grade students described difficulties caused by technical barriers; and upper-grade students more often described the recognition of patients’ emotions in conjunction with clinical experience. Theme 2, “From Mimicking AI to Autonomous Expression,” focuses on students’ reported experiences related to social skills, including direct application, recognition and adjustment, autonomous expression, and the simulation gap that persisted throughout the process. Theme 3, “From Technical Frustration to Mental Rehearsal,” integrates experiences related to self-management, self-awareness, and self-motivation. The three themes correspond to different dimensions of emotional intelligence, with students in different grade levels reporting distinct experiential characteristics. Conclusion Nursing undergraduates in different grades exhibit distinct experiential characteristics when using generative artificial intelligence to learn about emotional intelligence. Students’ reports repeatedly highlighted moderate tension around technological motivation, the ability to critically integrate technology, and the perceived value of technological friction. Based on these exploratory findings, we propose several preliminary educational implications—including grade-level-specific support, curriculum exploration, and education in critical technological literacy and ethics—for consideration in future research and practice.

items.title: Exploring Platformic Torque in Secondhand Market Platform Work
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents findings from an ethnographic study of online fashion reselling, an understudied form of gig work where individuals sell secondhand clothing on marketplace platforms. Unlike gig work models where labor is explicitly priced as a service, reselling embeds labor in the procurement, preparation, and sale of goods. We focus on Poshmark, a popular marketplace with 30 million US users, to examine how it mediates reseller labor within broader gendered, classed, and racialized dynamics of precarious work and fashion consumerism. Drawing on infrastructure studies, we extend the concept of torque to analyze how platforms structure reseller experiences across aesthetic, temporal, and regulatory dimensions. Through ethnographic narratives, we illustrate how Poshmark’s sociotechnical mechanisms shape experiences and aspirations of this kind of gig work. Our findings contribute to platform labor research by foregrounding intersectional pressures in marketplace platform work, expanding current understandings of gig economies beyond service work.

items.title: Exploring the impact of legislative absences on the working environment of gig workers in South Africa
items.abstract: This study pursues two objectives. Empirically, it examines how legislative exclusion is produced in South Africa and how gig workers experience it in their everyday working lives. Theoretically, it develops an interpretive account of the relationship between political and economic processes that are ordinarily treated as separate domains, reading political and regulatory exclusion as constitutive of the forms of economic insecurity and precarity that participants describe rather than as their determinant. The study is framed by the concept of legislative exclusion, understood as the process through which state action constitutes a category of workers as falling outside the scope of labor law; precarity, platform capitalism and algorithmic management are used to elaborate the processes through which that exclusion operates and the conditions with which it is associated. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 purposively sampled gig workers in Johannesburg working across e-hailing, delivery, freelancing and content creation, and the data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The sample spans two structurally distinct segments of platform labor, which are analyzed separately throughout: location-based work (e-hailing and delivery), which is geographically tethered, capital-intensive for the worker and in principle regulable by the national state; and remote online work (digital freelancing and social media content creation), which is contracted across borders and mediated by clients and monetization programs rather than by dispatch algorithms. The analysis reads exclusion as actively produced rather than merely absent: a statutory definition of the employee that platform work is arranged to fall outside, a jurisdictional architecture that renders the responsible corporate entity difficult to reach, and a recent transport regulation that recognizes e-hailing while leaving the employment relationship untouched. These instruments do not bear on the two segments equally: the transport regulation reaches location-based drivers alone, whereas remote online workers are addressed by no domestic instrument at all. Exclusion is in turn bound up with unbounded working hours, exclusion from employment benefits and the absence of any accessible dispute-resolution forum, though it is lived differently in each segment. Location-based participants described unreviewable deactivation and the transfer of vehicle, fuel and licensing costs; online participants described client non-payment, unenforceable informal agreements and dependence on opaque monetisation and visibility rules. The study contributes an interpretive account in which legislative exclusion is understood as a structuring condition through which risk is transferred to workers, platform and client authority is rendered unreviewable, and disadvantage is compounded over time.

items.title: Exploring the Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities: Implications for Digital Mental Health Services
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services presents novel opportunities for clinical assessment, therapeutic intervention, and continuous rehabilitation. Grounded in dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems theories, this study evaluates strategic pathways for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities into Digital Mental Health Services, analyzes core bioethical and data privacy challenges, and examines the prospective impact of immersive virtual environments on patient engagement and therapeutic outcomes. Methods: An iterative three-round Delphi inquiry was conducted with an international panel of 36 multidisciplinary experts spanning clinical psychiatry, Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities software development, digital ethics, and healthcare policy. Standardized, neutral visual scenarios prompted expert evaluations across 14 Digital Mental Health Services sub-areas. Panel consensus, rating dispersion, and domain interrelationships were quantified using Kendall’s coefficient of concordance (W), non-parametric Spearman rank-order correlation analysis, and descriptive dispersion metrics (median, interquartile range, standard deviation), complemented by reflexive thematic qualitative synthesis. Results: Expert agreement converged significantly from Round 1 to Round 3. High consensus emerged for AI-enhanced initial screening (mean = 4.7, SD = 0.5) and comprehensive VR assessments (mean = 4.5, SD = 0.8). While AI-managed crisis services showed high perceived probability (95%), findings highlighted the necessity of strict human-in-the-loop architectures over full autonomy to mitigate psychiatric triage hazards. Conclusions: Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Realities present viable adjunctive pathways for personalized psychiatric assessment and therapy, provided that systems implement strict clinician-in-the-loop safeguards, real-time dynamic consent, and end-to-end data encryption. Utilizing a Dynamic Capabilities framework enables healthcare organizations to systematically sense technological innovations, seize clinical opportunities, and reconfigure governance structures, thereby ensuring equitable, safe, and ethical digital mental health delivery.

items.title: Externalizing Epistemic Governance from Stateless Clinical LLMs: Why It Is Necessary and Why It Must Be Constrained
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models are increasingly embedded in clinical decision support, but they are stateless. They preserve no epistemic commitments across contexts, identical cases can yield divergent outputs, and fluent generation can acquire de facto authority over what counts as evidence without any matching structure of responsibility. We argue that whether clinical AI can be trusted and held accountable depends on where epistemic authority sits and who governs it, not on how well the model performs or how fluently it generates. From this it follows that epistemic governance has to be externalized from the model. It also has to be constrained, because relocating authority into a second generative layer reproduces the original problem. We make the claim concrete with a non-agentic, constraint-based architecture, instantiated in oncology. Context classification, evidence authority, and truth-state assignment are settled by dedicated, inspectable layers before any generation occurs; the language model is confined to bounded extraction and summarization. The central move is to keep deontic authority, what is permitted and reimbursed, distinct from epistemic authority, what the evidence supports, so that a reimbursement or jurisdictional constraint is represented as an allocation decision rather than collapsed into an apparent clinical fact. Uncertainty, disagreement between authoritative sources, and clinician overrides are preserved as explicit, inspectable states. By settling authority before generation and keeping it inspectable, the architecture restores the structure of responsibility that fluent generation erodes: the exercise of authority becomes attributable, and the resulting recommendation can be contested rather than absorbed as plain clinical fact.

items.title: Factors Influencing the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools and Their Association with Employability Skills among Undergraduate and Postgraduate Student
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Claude have rapidly permeated higher education, fundamentally altering the ways in which students learn, conduct research, and prepare for careers. Despite their widespread availability, the extent to which students adopt these tools varies considerably, influenced by factors such as perceived usefulness, ease of use, AI literacy, trust, and ethical awareness. This study investigates the determinants of AI tool adoption among 300 undergraduate and postgraduate students and examines the association between AI tool adoption and perceived employability skills. Employing a quantitative, survey-based research design with a structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire, data were analysed using multiple linear regression, simple linear regression, and independent samples t-test. The multiple regression model explained 34.1% of the variance in AI adoption (R² = 0.341, F(5, 294) = 30.4, p < .001), with AI literacy emerging as the strongest predictor (β = 0.304, p < .001), followed by perceived ease of use (β = 0.269), trust in AI (β = 0.269), perceived usefulness (β = 0.263), and ethical awareness (β = 0.164). The simple regression demonstrated that AI adoption significantly predicted employability skills (R² = 0.349, β = 0.591, p < .001). Furthermore, postgraduate students exhibited significantly higher AI adoption levels than undergraduate students, t(298) = 2.74, p = .007, with a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.334). These findings underscore the necessity for educational institutions to integrate AI literacy training and responsible AI usage policies into curricula, thereby equipping students with the digital competencies demanded by AI-driven workplaces. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI adoption in higher education by integrating multiple adoption determinants within a single empirical framework and linking them to employability outcomes.

items.title: Factors that facilitate artificial intelligence integration into global talent management: A systematic review
items.abstract: Orientation: Digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), are rapidly transforming human resource functions by enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of human resource practices. Research purpose: This systematic review examines the factors that facilitate the integration of AI into global talent management (GTM) and explores how these factors collectively inform theory on technology-enabled talent management systems. Motivation for the study: Research on the use of AI in GTM remains limited, and its theoretical implications are not yet well established. Research approach/design and method: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. The review encompassed eight databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, Emerald Insight, Sabinet and Elsevier) using a comprehensive and structured search strategy. Peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2020 and 2025 were screened. Twenty-three empirical studies meeting the inclusion criteria were subjected to full-text analysis. Main findings: The analysis revealed that AI integration into GTM is influenced by several interconnected enablers, including the strategic alignment of AI with talent objectives, adequate capabilities and digital infrastructure, ethical and governance frameworks and organisational readiness for implementation. Practical/managerial implications: Human resources practitioners and policymakers should adopt a systemic, integrative approach that aligns AI tools with organisational talent objectives. Contribution/value-add: This review advances theoretical discourse by integrating fragmented evidence into a cohesive understanding of the conditions that support AI-driven GTM. It offers a conceptual foundation for future research seeking to build theory at the intersection of AI, GTM and strategic human resource management.

items.title: FEATURES OF USING THE MATERIALS CREATED BY GENERATIVE MODELS FOR ADVERTISING IN UKRAINE AND WORLDWIDE
items.abstract: The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the use of generative artificial intelligence (hereinafter – AI) in the creation of visual advertising content and its impact on contemporary marketing practices in Ukraine and abroad. It is demonstrated that the integration of AI-generated photo and video materials transforms not only the set of advertising tools but also the very logic of organizing the advertising process, reshaping the balance between creative, managerial, and technological components. Generative models form a new type of creative environment in which content production becomes fast, flexible, and data-driven, allowing for scalability without a proportional increase in the costs. The study systematizes the key areas of application of generative AI in advertising, including the personalization of visual messages, production optimization, the development of dynamic formats, and the use of data-driven storytelling. At the same time, it is identified that technological advantages are accompanied by a number of risks related to the standardization of creative solutions, dependence on the quality of input data and on external technological infrastructure, the weakening of brand distinctiveness, and an increased likelihood of ethical and legal violations. It is argued that in the absence of adequate managerial control, generative content may lose strategic alignment with brand positioning and the long-term objectives of the enterprise. Special attention is paid to the Ukrainian context, which is characterized by the combination of rapid adoption of AI solutions with human resource, institutional, and regulatory constraints intensified by wartime conditions. It is shown that under these circumstances generative artificial intelligence performs a dual role: on the one hand, it acts as a tool for improving the effectiveness of marketing communications; on the other hand, it requires clearly defined frameworks for responsible use. The article concludes that generative AI should be viewed as a driver of structural change in the advertising industry, the effectiveness of which depends on its integration into marketing management systems, the quality of managerial decision-making, compliance with ethical principles and legal requirements, and the ability of brands to maintain their distinct character.
